analysis.one_liner: Funds pilot programs testing benefits that follow gig and independent workers between jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate committee without ever getting a vote, despite sponsorship from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Department of Labor to hand out about $20 million in competitive grants to states, local governments, and nonprofits. The money was for designing, testing, and evaluating "portable benefits" — things like health coverage, disability, workers' compensation, and paid savings accounts for the growing number of independent contractors, freelancers, and temporary workers who don't get benefits through an employer. A government watchdog office would have evaluated the results and reported back to Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent workers — freelancers, gig drivers, contractors, and temporary workers — who currently receive no employer benefits and often lose coverage entirely when they change jobs. If the pilots proved a model worked, it could have laid groundwork for nationwide portable benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Sets up a competitive grant program run by the Department of Labor for fiscal year 2023, funding both new models and evaluation or improvement of existing ones for portable benefits [S2][S3].

Defines portable benefits to include workers' compensation, skills training, disability coverage, health insurance, retirement saving, income security, and short-term saving for workers outside traditional full-time employment [S3].
Excludes retirement-only plans from grant funding, pushing states and nonprofits toward broader benefit packages [S2][S3].
Requires the Government Accountability Office to evaluate the grants and report on their impact on workers' pay by September 30, 2025, so Congress could learn what works before scaling up [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the $20 million in grants ($5 million for improving existing models, $15 million for new ones). The bill authorizes but does not appropriate the money, and it imposes no direct new obligation on any company.

drawbacks.text: The bill is small and experimental: it authorizes only $20 million and creates no actual benefits for any worker — nothing would change for independent workers unless a pilot led to later legislation [S3].
The money is authorized but not automatically appropriated, so even a passed version of the bill could have gone unfunded without a separate spending action [S3].

Critics of portable-benefit schemes argue that treating contractors like employees, even partially, blurs the line between employment and contracting and could raise costs for small businesses and platforms — a debate the pilots would have fed into.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A low-cost, low-risk experiment: $20 million to find out whether portable benefits can be made to work before Congress commits to anything larger. The main weakness is the opposite of overreach — it is so modest, and its funding so conditional, that even full passage would not have directly changed any worker's situation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Mark Warner introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, joined by five cosponsors from both parties: Senators Young (R-IN), King (I-ME), Cramer (R-ND), Bennet (D-CO), and Hoeven (R-ND) [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo holds. Independent workers are no closer to employer-style benefits, and companies that hire contractors and gig workers face no movement toward contributing to their benefits. Taxpayers also avoided a $20 million experimental outlay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies using contractor and gig labor

for.name: Sen. Mark Warner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Portable Benefits for Independent Workers Pilot Program Act on May 18, 2023 [S1][S5].

for.name: Sens. Todd Young, Angus King, Kevin Cramer, Michael Bennet, and John Hoeven
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, making the bill one of the few labor bills with backing from both parties [S4][S5].

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die at the end of the 118th Congress [S5].

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 118th Congress, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (three Republicans, one Independent, one Democrat) with no recorded opposition, so no party split ever formed — the bill simply never moved.

industries.industry: Gig and app-based platform companies (ride-hail, delivery, freelance marketplaces)
industries.note: These companies hire workers as contractors precisely so they do not pay for benefits. A pilot program is only a research step, but successful models from it could later require platforms to contribute to workers' health, disability, or income benefits, which is why portable-benefit proposals draw industry resistance. In this case the threat never advanced.

industries.industry: Temporary staffing and labor contracting agencies
industries.note: Their business model also relies on workers outside traditional employment arrangements; portable benefit models could add contribution costs. No action occurred, so no effect took hold.
